newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's foreign minister threatens to quit.
newsitem.headline: Israel's foreign minister threatens to quit.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy brought Benjamin Netanyahu's fractious coalition closer to collapse on Monday, threatening to resign over the way the prime minister runs the government.
After brooding for several days, Levy broke a public silence and launched scathing criticism of how a government that has lurched from crisis to crisis operates.

"I am considering my actions and weighing if there is truly a possibility that these things will be rectified, that the government will be able to operate, that it will stick to the peace process," Levy, 59, said in measured tones.
"After considering all these things in the coming days I will decide on my next moves, on my continuing membership in the government," he told a hastily called news conference.

The disclosure on Friday that National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon had met in June with top PLO official Mahmoud Abbas -- a secret which Netanyahu did not share with his foreign minister -- triggered Levy's threat.

"If I had known, I would have encouraged minister Sharon to meet not only with Abu Mazen (Abbas' nom de guerre), but with everyone," said Levy. "The question is, whether as foreign minister I should know things after the fact."

Levy said he and his Gesher faction, which has five of the 66 coalition seats in the 120-member parliament, joined the government to move the peace process with the Palestinians forward and improve life for low-income Israelis.
"I am sorry to say that a year after the government was established, the peace process is stuck and the social situation has deteriorated," he said.

"Where is the government going? Is the government going to advance the peace process? Yes or no? The government was formed to make decisions," he said. "As long as we try to plaster things over, the crisis will not be solved."
If Gesher legislators leave the government, Netanyahu's fate would depend on a slim majority of one in parliament, hanging on the strained loyalty of rebellious members of his Likud party.

Last week 11 coalition members, angry at what they see as Netanyahu's autocratic style, withheld their support for him in a parliamentary no-confidence motion he narrowly survived following the resignation of Finance Minister Dan Meridor.

Netanyahu planned to appoint Sharon to the post but Levy balked at the former general's subsequent demand to join him, the prime minister and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai in an inner cabinet team that shapes peace policy.
Levy appeared to offer Netanyahu a way out at the news conference. The so-called "kitchen cabinet" should be scrapped and all major decisions made by the full cabinet, he said.

"The prime minister did not hear from me any opposition for minister Ariel Sharon to be a partner...he did hear from me that there is no room for the kitchen cabinet," Levy said. "(Its) existence is not healthy."
Netanyahu responded to Levy's challenge in a brief statement that gave only a little ground to his demands.

"In reaction to the comments of the foreign minister, the prime minister reiterated he has faith in the foreign minister and that he intends to consult him soon on government moves. At this stage no meetings have been set," the statement said.
Shimon Shiffer, political correspondent of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, predicted intensive efforts by Netanyahu to resolve the crisis.
"The next two days will be devoted to reconciliation and turning David Levy around," Shiffer said. "Everyone will promise everything to everyone -- until the next crisis."
